newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Group aims to rehone Taiwan's competitive edge.
newsitem.headline: Group aims to rehone Taiwan's competitive edge.

text.p: Six business leaders formed a blue-ribbon private panel on Monday to explore ways to boost Taiwan's competitiveness at a time of mounting international pressure and slowing local economic growth.
The committee was inaugurated and chaired by Jeffrey Koo of Taiwan's influential Chinese National Association of Industry and Commerce.
Koo said Taiwan's slowing "Asian dragon" economy needed a breakthrough to rebuild its competitiveness.
"Taiwan's economy is at a bottleneck and facing strong competition from foreign countries," Koo said.

He said the first thing government should do is to revise business law and regulations to create a suitable environment for stronger investment. Increasing efficiency in the Legislative Yuan, or parliament, is a must, he said.
"There are ways we can measure our Legislative Yuan's efficiency, like how many bills it passes per year in comparison to other countries," Koo said.
Koo said the government should expedite infrastructure construction and enact favorable legislation to encourage private investment.
Premier and Vice-President Lien Chan hailed the new body, saying the private sector could boost Taiwan's development.
"Private sector production value comprises 81 percent of all economic value, so it plays an important role in both investment and production," Lien told the inaugural meeting.
Taiwan aims to leap into the ranks of the world's five most competitive economies by 2000, up from the mid-teens now.
Another co-founder, chairman Kao Chin-yen of the Chinese National Federation of Industries, singled out tax reform as the key to reigniting Taiwan's once-sizzling economy.
"I think the tax reform is the first thing the government should work on," Kao said to reporters.
Taiwan is preparing to merge the island's business income tax and personal income tax into a single 25 percent levy to address complaints from business that the dual system was cumbersome and unfair.
The personal income tax is 40 percent for the highest brackets while the current business income tax is 25 percent.
